archetype: Five-colour Dragon typal ramp-midrange: accelerate, land fat fliers, and convert with per-Dragon entry triggers or by multiplying one attacking Dragon. The frame and the composition now AGREE, which is a change since the previous version of this document. strategic_frame.json was rewritten without an archetype keyword and today's deck-audit reports archetype null, source 'none — base targets apply'; the old complaint that the frame declared 'combo' and the audit inherited a tutors-4-8 / protection-4-6 template is discharged and has been deleted rather than annotated. Read every axis below against the BASE targets, which is what the audit used.
verdict: Above the mana line this deck is in good shape and the pilot is right about it; below the line it is five lands short of the corpus's 36–38 — and the table corroborates the KIND of claim without pricing the number, because a 100-game correlation between resource development and winning sets no land count. open_questions[2] routes that half to the goldfish. In 100 seeded Forge games against the pilot's pod it won 12 — 0.12, ci95 [0.070, 0.198], n=100 — and made 5.48 land drops a game (ci95 [5.15, 5.81], n=100), and inside that sample what separates its wins from its losses is RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT — land drops and the casts they buy. Sweeping all eighteen numeric per-seat fields the record keeps per game, the partition is NINE separating with a Welch interval excluding zero, EIGHT null, and ONE untestable — `eliminated_turn`, which cannot separate wins from losses even in principle because a winner is never eliminated (all twelve wins carry null). Exactly two of the nine are resource counts rather than consequences of having won: land drops (7.25 against 5.24, diff 2.01, ci95 [0.52, 3.50], p 0.0002) and casts (15.92 against 9.02, diff 6.89, ci95 [2.28, 11.51], p 0.0001). The other seven are downstream. First-attack timing is one of the eight nulls; turns survived is null too but is a quantity I derived, not a field the record keeps. Both nulls this document previously enumerated are non-resource, which is why 'land drops' alone read as exclusive when it was not. lean_into[3] decides whether the two are one finding or two and shows the working — all of it under Forge's own caveat that its AI is "best with aggro and midrange decks, poor to ok in control decks, pretty bad for most combo decks" and that every seat including ours is that AI. The binding axis is mana-base, 31 land copies against a 36–38 floor, with land drops falling 0.834 / 0.670 / 0.525 across turns three to five while 26 maindeck nonland entries cost five or more. The conversion above it is better evidenced than it has ever been: four presentable checker-passed stacks now rather than three, and stack 002's annotation establishes that the deck CAN kill a fresh 40-life seat — the claim this document previously carried the other way round.

lean_into.what: Build toward the Dragon Tempest board and widen its three-card damage leg.
lean_into.why: Three checker-passed, non-withheld boards now bear on this plan and none bears on the other. Stack 001: fifteen Faerie Dragon tokens enter as one event, Dragon Tempest triggers fifteen times at X=17, and its final_state kills the 30-life seat on the second trigger and the 38-life seat if three triggers were aimed there — 255 damage available. Stack 002: one Lathliss cast under Miirym, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest deals 64 damage in 12 separately-targeted instances, kills the 32-life seat, AND — per the annotation added beside its byte-identical checker-passed summary — can kill a fresh 40-life seat instead, because all twelve instances read 'any target' and may every one name the same player: 6, 12, 16, 20, 26, 32, 37, 42, with that seat at 3 before the eighth so nothing fizzles. Stack 007 is 002's board minus Panharmonicon and settles the sibling question. Against that, no passing stack names any combat-kill multiplier. The rates agree with the evidence: THE ENTRY KILL 0.240 assembled / 0.153 by turn six against THE COMBAT KILL's 0.204 / 0.128 — 3.6 points apart, both UNVERIFIED by their own labels, and never to be summed or averaged. What none of it proves: 001 grants the payoff, the connection and a d20 fixed at 15; 002 and 007 grant four and three permanents already on the battlefield with eight lands.

citations.quote: Value is not a win.

lean_into.what: HOLD PANHARMONICON. This reverses a cut this document previously proposed.
lean_into.why: The evidence that entry named as absent has arrived and it points the other way. Checker-passed stack 007 resolves stack 002's exact board with Panharmonicon removed and nothing else changed: Miirym triggers once instead of twice, ONE token copy enters instead of two, and the cascade produces 20 damage in 4 instances instead of 64 in 12 — 20 of 64, a 68.75% loss, because the doubler was doubling Terror and both Dragon Tempest abilities on every entry as well as Miirym. The 32-life seat survives at 12, and 007's checker verified the margin cannot be closed: the only activated ability on the board other than the lands' mana abilities is the {1}{R} Dragon pump, the scenario's declared six mana pays Lathliss's eminence-reduced five and leaves exactly {1} against a two-mana cost, and partial payments are not allowed. So cutting Panharmonicon costs stack 002 its LETHALITY, not its margin, and among the four presentable checker-passed stacks it is the only board that both CASTS its Dragon from hand and can kill a fresh 40-life seat — 001 kills a 30-life and a 38-life seat but casts nothing and grants a completed combat connection with a d20 fixed at 15, 005 cheats Drakuseth in with Sneak Attack for 17 and kills nobody, and 007 casts the same Lathliss for 20. The mana argument against it is real — four mana, no board, no mana, on the binding axis — and it is outweighed: the pod run measures this deck dealing a MEDIAN of 12.0 combat damage a game (mean 26.30, ci95 [18.82, 33.78], n=100, 22 games at zero). A deck that short of damage does not spend a proven kill for a land.

citations.quote: Value is not a win.

lean_into.what: Buy one-shot mana and cost reduction, not more average mana.
lean_into.why: The measurement shows the mechanism exactly: model_treasures took the commander from cast-by-turn-six 0.0% to 4.1% and 'never cast' from 9,175 to 7,170 of 10,000 while mean available mana stayed identical at 4.219 on turn five. A deck with 26 maindeck entries at mana value five or more does not need a higher average; it needs one turn that spikes. The repo has already tested the alternative on this deck and it failed: twelve spells swapped for twelve averaging three mana cheaper moved turn-five mana by 0.02, while three lands and four cheap accelerants moved it +0.27 and bought seven points of turn-five land drop.

lean_into.what: You are not the archenemy at this table — and you are not the slowest deck at it either. Both seats that win this table out-drop you on land drops with disjoint intervals, and the one seat you are level with wins less than you do — and what separates your own wins is resource development rather than the attack step.
lean_into.why:
THE POD, ENUMERATED ON EVERY SEAT. Combat damage TAKEN, all four: giada-angels 13.13 (ci95 [9.80, 16.46]), ur-dragon 21.99 ([17.12, 26.86]), baylen-tokens 31.49 ([27.24, 35.74]), vito 42.59 ([33.40, 51.78]). Ur-dragon is SECOND-lowest, not lowest — giada takes less and wins 39 — so low damage taken is not itself an advantage and the pod is not focusing this seat. PACE, all four, which the previous version of this entry compared only against another deck's run and therefore over-claimed: first attack ur-dragon 20.38 (ci95 [18.98, 21.79], n=81), vito 19.22 ([17.36, 21.08], n=69), baylen 18.67 ([17.27, 20.06], n=51), giada 13.28 ([12.29, 14.28], n=95). Per-game against ours — diff_means(opponent, ours), so a positive difference means WE attack later — only giada separates: diff +7.0985, ci95 [+5.3750, +8.8220], p 0.0001. Vito (diff +1.1653, ci95 [-1.1683, +3.4990], p 0.331) and baylen (diff +1.7160, ci95 [-0.2643, +3.6964], p 0.11) do not. The baylen interval was printed as [-3.70, 0.26] until this revision — the other orientation's, and the last surviving site of the sign defect recorded in gaps; its two neighbours were already right, and the two p-values are restated in this orientation as well, because permutation_p depends on argument order. 'Slowest deck at the table' is therefore false and is withdrawn; what survives is slower than giada, indistinguishable from vito and baylen, and second-lowest on damage taken. RESOURCES, all four: land drops ur-dragon 5.48 ([5.15, 5.81]), giada 6.79 ([6.31, 7.27]), vito 6.43 ([6.01, 6.85]), baylen 5.17 ([4.89, 5.45]). Both seats above us have disjoint intervals from ours and between them take 81 of the 100 wins; the one seat we are level with, baylen, takes 7. That is the same finding as the within-our-games one, arriving from the pod side. 

WITHIN OUR OWN GAMES, WITH THE SET NAMED FIRST AND THE PARTITION BALANCED. The record keeps eighteen numeric fields per seat per game. Every figure below is diff_means(losses, wins), ONE orientation throughout, so a positive difference means wins are higher; the previous version of this paragraph mixed two orientations and printed three intervals with the sign reversed. 18 = 9 + 8 + 1. NINE separate with an interval excluding zero: lands, casts, triggers, combat damage dealt to players, noncombat damage dealt to players, token resolutions, token attackers, commander damage max, and combat damage taken — that last one in the OTHER direction (23.97 in losses against 7.50 in wins, diff -16.47, ci95 [-23.35, -9.58]). EIGHT are null: activations, tokens observed, token blockers, token combat damage to players, tokens chumped, creatures lost, token damage share, and first attack (diff -1.62, ci95 [-4.87, 1.63]). ONE is UNTESTABLE rather than null, and the distinction matters: `eliminated_turn` is null in all twelve wins because a winner is never eliminated, so the field cannot separate the two groups even in principle and no test of it means anything. Seven of the nine are consequences of having won and cannot be read as causes — you deal damage, generate triggers and attack with tokens BECAUSE the game went your way. Exactly two sit upstream of all of it: lands (7.25 against 5.24, diff 2.01, ci95 [0.52, 3.50], p 0.0002) and casts (15.92 against 9.02, diff 6.89, ci95 [2.28, 11.51], p 0.0001). One further null is worth naming although it is NOT one of the eighteen, because this document leaned on it: turns survived (8.72 against 9.42, diff 0.70, ci95 [-0.66, 2.06]) is a quantity I derived from `eliminated_turn` and `global_turn`, not a field the record keeps. 

ONE FINDING OR TWO — UNDECIDED BY THIS SAMPLE, AND HERE IS THE WORKING. Lands and casts correlate at Pearson r 0.6289 over the 100 games (r-squared 0.3956), so they share about two fifths of their variance and three fifths is unshared. The test that would separate them is residualising each against the other by OLS (casts = -0.5653 + 1.9006 x lands; lands = 3.4299 + 0.2081 x casts), and it kills BOTH — all three intervals below are diff_means(losses, wins), the same orientation as everything else in this entry. Casts after lands: -0.37 in losses against 2.70 in wins, diff +3.0711, ci95 [-0.9446, +7.0868]. Lands after casts: -0.07 against 0.51, diff +0.5765, ci95 [-0.7112, +1.8642]. The simplest normalisation agrees — casts per land drop, 1.73 against 2.24, diff +0.5022, ci95 [-0.0010, +1.0053], which includes zero by a thousandth at the low end. Not one of the three excludes zero, so at twelve wins this sample CANNOT tell the two apart, and the finding is reported as undecided rather than resolved. For the purposes of this document I LEAD ON LANDS, and the reason is not the residual test: land drops survive excluding the fourteen clock games, are corroborated from the pod side by two seats with disjoint intervals above us, and the 36-38 target never rested on the simulation at all. What I will not bury is which way the residuals lean — permutation p is 0.0121 for casts-after-lands against 0.1553 for lands-after-casts, and deck-skeptic sized the lean at 76.5% of detectable for casts-after-lands against 44.8% for lands-after-casts. That is a lean, not a finding, and open_questions[5] is where it goes rather than into a prescription. 

WHERE THE LEAN POINTS, AND WHY THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT FOLLOW IT. If casts carries signal independent of lands, the deck-side thing that turns one turn's mana into more spells is COST REDUCTION — and that is this document's own second single point of failure: four cards (Urza's Incubator, Herald's Horn, Dragonspeaker Shaman, Dragonlord's Servant), 25.8% of openers against the corpus's 31%-at-five, 0.518 assembled and 0.419 by turn six, with the crossed reducer-plus-ramp hand at 0.417 and 0.285. It is UNFUNDED: all six adds below go to mana-base, colour-sources and interaction-breadth, and not one of them adds a fifth reducer. Saying so plainly is the point — the previous version of this paragraph wrote 'no new prescription follows', which dressed an UNDECIDED test up as a settled negative, and that is the wrong shape of sentence for a test that came back at 76.5% of detectable. Two reasons it is routed rather than prescribed, and the second is mechanical rather than a matter of taste. First, nothing may be sized off a lean; the SPOF stands on its own engine evidence and would be worth funding even if the residual test had come back flat. Second, this document's own rule is that an add must MOVE the axis it names, and I recomputed both closers this engine block already lists against (cards, roles): Goreclaw, Terror of Qal Sisma carries `ramp:cost-reduction` and moves ramp 21 to 22 — further OVER a band this document argues at axes[6] must not be cut — while Morophon, the Boundless, which is the bigger reducer by far, carries only `payoff:typal` and `threat:body` and moves NO computable axis at all. So the better card is invisible to every measure the gate can check and the visible one moves the wrong way. That is a defect in the measure rather than in the cards, it is not something to paper over with a swap nobody gets to review, and open_questions[5] routes it. 

LIMITS THE RECORD STATES ITSELF. 26 of the 63 attributed eliminations of our seat were by LIFE LOSS, which no blocker and no race answers. Every seat is Forge's AI, "best with aggro and midrange decks, poor to ok in control decks, pretty bad for most combo decks". Both resource results survive dropping the 14 games that ran to the 300-second clock (rule: ms >= 300000; lands diff +2.1419, ci95 [+0.6469, +3.6369], p 0.0002; casts diff +7.6464, ci95 [+3.0278, +12.2650], p 0.0001, n=12 wins and 74 losses). And this is correlation inside one seeded AI-vs-AI sample, not a causal claim and not a rate for any other table.

THE STRONGEST FIGURES IN THIS DOCUMENT ARE MINE, NOT THE RECORD'S, and they are flagged rather than smuggled. The run record publishes the seat's `lands` mean (5.48, ci95 [5.15, 5.81], n=100) and its `casts` mean (9.85, ci95 [8.84, 10.86], n=100) but neither split by outcome. Everything in lean_into[3]'s second and third paragraphs was computed by me from the record's own per-game `games[].per_seat['ur-dragon']` values using manamap.sim.stats.diff_means and permutation_p (seeded at 0, 10,000 iterations, so it replays): the eighteen-field partition, the win/loss splits on lands and casts, the eight nulls, the one untestable field, the Pearson r, the two OLS residuals and the clock-drop robustness check. ORIENTATION IS PART OF THE CLAIM, and it is stated because getting it wrong is how the previous revision shipped three intervals with the sign reversed while the conclusion they supported was correct: every figure is `diff_means(losses, wins)` and `permutation_p(losses, wins)`, so a positive difference means wins are higher, and an interval on a difference must contain that difference — the check that catches this in one glance. The argument order also changes the permutation p, because the test shuffles the pooled list and the pool is built as xs + ys, so every p here is quoted from that one orientation and no other. Two further things a reader should hold against those p-values: permutation_p is floored at 1/(10,000+1) by Phipson & Smyth, so a printed 0.0001 means 'no more extreme rearrangement was found' rather than one in ten thousand; and with twelve wins the interval, not the p, is the claim — which is why the residual test is reported as UNDECIDED rather than as a decision between lands and casts. All of it is correlation inside one AI-vs-AI sample of 100 seeded games, not a causal claim and not a rate for any other table.

The run corroborates the KIND of claim the mana-base axis makes and prices no COUNT. A correlation between resource development and winning is silent on whether the right number is 33, 36 or 38 lands; the 36–38 comes from strategy:deckbuilding.ratios and Burgess's 45 sources, both cited above, and open_questions[2] is what routes the count to a model that can price it. Nothing in this document infers a land count from the simulation.

Fourteen of the 100 games ran to the 300-second clock. The record's own assumption is that a game past the clock is recorded as a draw rather than dropped, and `won_by` reports 'all opponents have lost' 100 times while some outcomes carry an empty `lost` map — so a fraction of the sample is a truncated game read as a finish. No figure here was corrected for it and no figure here excludes those games.

A controlled A/B is the right check on the whole prescription and the diagnosis schema cannot route it: `settled_by` accepts only resolve-stack, research-strategy and goldfish. The run to make is `manamap pilot experiment ur-dragon --a <the current version> --b <the 36-land version> --vs giada-angels vito baylen-tokens`, on the pod this diagnosis reads, and the figures to compare are win rate, lands and first attack turn with their intervals.

One logged game is texture, not a rate. Entry 001's Blood Moon lockout is the reason this audit was asked for and is not evidence about the mana base's normal behaviour — no figure in this diagnosis comes from it, and the pilot has CLOSED that direction ('I am not calling this a deck problem in the sense of needing an answer to Blood Moon'), so nothing here proposes one. The rates come from the 10,000-iteration goldfish and the 100-game pod run, the counts from deck-audit and cards.json, the colour figures from mana_analysis.json, and the bracket from bracket_report.json.

This document cites no card list and no figure from engine.json. That policy was set when the file was failing its validator; `validate-engine ur-dragon` returns OK today (7 stages, 95 cards placed, 0 unassigned, 4 of 13 lines verified by a passing stack) and the policy was kept anyway rather than revisited, so the engine block above is built from deck-audit's priced components and goldfish_targets.json alone. A reader wanting the engine's own view should read that file, not this block.

card_roles.json classifies 96.8% of this deck — Chaos Warp, Rishkar's Expertise and Sneak Attack have no entry — so every role-derived axis count above is a floor by more than the usual margin, and the audit's own probe note names seven further cards whose card-advantage function the taxonomy filed elsewhere.

A CONTROLLED A/B IS THE RIGHT CHECK ON THE WHOLE PRESCRIPTION AND THE SCHEMA CANNOT ROUTE IT. `settled_by` accepts only resolve-stack, research-strategy and goldfish, so open_questions[6] routes the larger sample as `goldfish` and names the Forge command in its own text. The run that would actually price these six swaps is `manamap pilot experiment ur-dragon --a <the current version> --b <the 36-land version> --vs giada-angels vito baylen-tokens`, N per arm, comparing win rate, land drops, casts and first-attack turn with their intervals. Note what it cannot do: same seeds are not paired games, so the control is N.

THE ADD GATE CANNOT SEE THE DECK'S SECOND SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE, which is why one real hole in this prescription is routed rather than closed. `validate_diagnosis` recomputes only the seven role counts and `interaction-breadth`, and cost reduction has no axis of its own — it lands inside `ramp`, which this deck is deliberately OVER on.
